title: Turn the hearts (Malachi 4:5–6)
hook: the last lines of the Protestant Old Testament: hearts of parents turned to children

segments.voice: Yesterday, ani: Zechariah's lowly king, riding a donkey instead of a warhorse. Your line: lowly, riding.

In a Protestant Bible, the Old Testament ends with Malachi. Turn the page, and the next thing is the first line of Matthew, a list of names. Between them sits a silence the Bible doesn't fill. So whatever Malachi says last stands right at the seam. You might expect a grand vision, or a thunderclap. Instead, the final words are about something small and close to home. Families. Parents and children. Who's speaking to whom, and who isn't.

Malachi's name means my messenger, and it may be a title rather than a name. His book is a series of arguments between God and the people, about tired worship, broken promises and marriages, and the poor being cheated. Then the end, in the King James Bible: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD: And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers." Elijah doesn't die in 2 Kings; he's carried up in a whirlwind. So the hope grew that he'd come back, to prepare the way for God. At the Passover seder, Jewish tradition pours a cup for Elijah and opens the door for him. And look at Elijah's work: not defeating enemies, but mending families, turning hearts across the generations, both ways. Then the very last words warn that otherwise God will strike the land with a curse. That ending is so hard that in synagogue readings the verse before it is read again afterward, so the book closes on Elijah and hope. These words come back soon. In the opening chapter of Luke, an angel promises that a child named John will come in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children. Christians read John the Baptist as the Elijah Malachi promised. So the Old Testament, in this arrangement, ends with a family reunion still waiting to happen.
screen: then, large: `HE SHALL TURN THE HEART OF THE FATHERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone a generation away from you, a parent or a child, or if they're gone or far away, a grandparent, a niece, a mentor, and notice what's between you: warmth, distance, an old hurt, a thing unsaid. Don't try to fix it all; just let your heart turn toward them a few degrees, the way Malachi pictures it. If you pray, bring them before God by name; if not, simply hold them in mind with care.
Malachi, meaning my messenger: his last promise that Elijah would come and turn the hearts of parents to children, and children to parents.
Your line: open the door for Elijah. Hearts turn both ways, parents and children alike. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some churches read Malachi in Advent, as the prophecy of a messenger before the Lord, and pair it with the Gospel stories of John the Baptist.

chat.meaning: Malachi's last promise: Elijah will turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the children to their fathers. Mending families, both ways.

notes: Malachi 4:5–6 are 3:23–24 in Hebrew Bibles. In synagogue reading, 3:23 is repeated after 3:24 so as not to end on a curse; confirm.
'Roughly four centuries' between Malachi (c. 5th century BC) and the New Testament era; approximate and common. Confirm phrasing.
Whether 'Malachi' is a name or title ('my messenger', cf. 3:1) is debated; presented as 'may be'.

Canon order: Protestant OT ends with Malachi; Hebrew Bible ends with 2 Chronicles; Douay-Rheims and some Catholic/Orthodox Bibles place Maccabees or other books differently. Stated neutrally; confirm.
Elijah's cup and opening the door at the seder: a neighbor's practice, mentioned without comparison.
